transcript: Well, if you ever wanted to see the hot priest from Fleabag play every character in a Chekhov play, I guess now's your chance. Andrew Scott is currently starring in a one man version of Uncle Vanya off Broadway. And this is particularly funny for me because I've now seen seven different versions of Uncle Vanya in nearly consecutive years. Which is fine by me because I love the play. I think it's by contrast. I saw the show with my friend, who went in knowing absolutely nothing about Uncle Vanya. And I asked her afterward if she had any trouble following who was who and what was going on. And she said that she followed it just fine. They do make some creative choices with both the aging and the abridged script adaptation to make it clear what's going on. But of course, a lot of it is owed to the virtuosic performance from Andrew Scott himself, who really embodies all of these characters and gets inside their deep emotions while also being quite funny at times. In terms of the production overall, they take an approach here that is very understated and ruminative. Like, there's a lot of long pauses and at times pretty slow, quiet delivery of the text. And there are moments where that leads to some beautiful, emotionally devastating beats where we're really sitting with these characters in a profound state of grief and disappointment. But when most of the show is like that, except For, like, a couple key moments, I don't know, it starts to lose its potency and feel almost a little bit lethargic. I felt similarly about this as I did about Eddie Izzard's solo version of hamlet, where it's like, yeah, you're amazing. It's fun to see a. An extremely talented actor flex their skills, and maybe even worth seeing the show for that alone, especially if you're a fan of the actor, which I am, but I'm also a big fan of hamlet and a big fan of Uncle Vanya. And I was sort of left doubting whether this solo show format actually served the text. And I gotta be honest, if it was meant to elucidate or reinterpret anything in the play, it was not in a way that resonated with me personally. Also, like, even if you can follow along and keep the characters apart, like, it's not as easy, it's not the most user friendly viewing experience. It sort of feels like creating a problem for yourself to solve, but without much reward. Like digging a hole in the ground just to show you can climb your way back up, but at the end of the day, you're still on ground level.
